text.0_Chapter, 0_Tosefta: We ask for the rains until Nissan is over, as it says, "And rain will fall for you, the earlier and latter rains during the first [month] (Yoel 2);" [these are] the words of Rabbi Meir. And the Sages say,"Earlier rains [fall in] Marcheshvan, and latter rains [fall on] the first of Nissan (and so these dates are the timetable for prayers for rain). Rabbi Meir said to them, "Knowing that a tree makes fruit for twelve [months], and produce [grows] for six months; what have we found with trees, as it says [about it], "By its month (meaning halfway through the month), it will bear (Yechezkel 47)," so too produce, at its fifteenth day [its season ends]. Haven't you learnt, that earlier and latter rains [fall throughout] Nissan.
text.0_Chapter, 1_Tosefta: From when do we start asking for rains? From when the time of the rains comes. If it was a lacking year (meaning, a year with 353 days as opposed to 354), we give it its lack (the extra day it should have had). If not, it goes according to its set schedule: [All of this goes by] the words of Rabbi [Yehudah haNasi]. Rabban Shimon ben Gamaliel says, "Actually, they go according to their set schedule [all the time]." If it was a leap year, we give it its extra.
text.0_Chapter, 2_Tosefta: What is considered the first rain (heb. R'viah)? [Rabbi Meir says, "An early one (lit. a firstborn) [falls] by the third [of Marcheshvan]; a middle one [falls] by the seventh; [and] a late one (lit. a dark one) [falls] by the seventeenth." Rabbi Yehudah says, "An early one [falls] by the seventh; a middle one [falls] by the seventeenth; [and] a late one [falls] by the twenty-third." Rabbi Yose says, An early one [falls] by the seventeenth; a middle one [falls] by the twenty-third; [and] a late one [falls] by Rosh Chodesh Kislev."] And so, Rabbi Yose would say, "The individuals do not fast until Rosh Chodesh Kislev."
text.0_Chapter, 3_Tosefta: What is considered the second rain? Once the [normal] time for rain has arrived, the words of Rabbi Meir. And the Sages say, once the [second] rain has fallen. Rabbi Yosei says, everything that depends on rainfall, once the [normal] time for rain has arrived; and for anything that does not depend on rainfall, once the second rain has fallen. Rabban Shimon ben Gamaliel says, [as to] rains than fell for seven days, one after another, without stopping, they are [considered to be] of sufficient quantity for second rain. How much rain must fall to be [considered to be] of sufficient quantity for second rain? [Enough] to fill a vessel of three handbreadths, the words of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehuda says, one [handbreadth] for the first, two for the second, and three for the "rains" (alt., "third rain"; see Lieberman). Said Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, there is no rain as to which each and every handbreadth from above is not countered by two handbreadths from [below] the earth, and thus it says (Ps. 42:8), "Depth calls to depth [at the roar of Your cataracts]." Why is it called r'viah? Because it fertilizes (rova'at) the earth.
text.0_Chapter, 4_Tosefta: All who said [that after the first three fasts of Kislev had passed without rain, then for the next three fasts] they may eat and drink while it is still day, [but] they are forbidden from working, bathing, and anointing, from wearing shoes (lit., "sandals"), [and] from marital relations (Taan. 1:6), the day is forbidden for work but the night is permitted. From where is it derived that the day follows after the night? As it is said (Esther 4:16), "Go assemble all the Jews who are found in Shushan... [Do not eat or drink for three days -- night and day]." All those who said [that for the three fasts ordained after the 17th of Cheshvan (Taan. 1:4)], they may eat and drink once it gets dark, [and] they are permitted in working, bathing, and anointing, and in wearing shoes, [and] in marital relations, they may eat and drink until eastern [horizon] can be seen, the words for Rebbi. Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon says, until the crow of the rooster. [But if] he slept and got up, he is forbidden immediately. All those who said they are forbidden from wearing shoes, one may put on shoes upon leaving a city, and remove them upon arriving to [another] city, and you may say the same regarding ostracism and mourning.
text.0_Chapter, 5_Tosefta: Who is an "individual" (i.e., one who can take it upon himself to fast for rain on behalf of the general public (see Taan. 1:4))? Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says, [not just] anyone who wishes to make himself an individual may do so -- [but] a Torah scholar may do so -- unless the Beit Din entrusts him on behalf of the general public. Rabban Shimon ben Gamaliel says, [in regards to] a matter of suffering, one who wishes to make himself an individual may do so, and a Torah scholar may [also] do so, and he will bring blessing upon himself. [But as to] a matter as to which one obtains a benefit, not anyone who wishes to make himself an individual may do so -- but a Torah scholar may do so -- unless the Beit Din entrusts him on behalf of the general public.
text.0_Chapter, 6_Tosefta: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar in the name of Rabbi Meir, and so too would Rabbi Dosa say according to his words: Half of Tishrei, Marcheshvan, and half of Kislev is the planting season. Half of Kislev, and Tevet, and half of Shevat is the winter. Half of Shevat, and Adar, and half of Nisan is the cold season. Half of Nisan, Iyar, and half of Sivan is the harvest season. Half of Sivan, Tammuz, and half of Av is the summer. Half of Av, Elul, and half of Tishrei is the hot season. Rabbi Yehuda would reckon [the seasons starting] from Marcheshvan. Rabbi Shimon reckons from Tishrei.
text.0_Chapter, 7_Tosefta: The order [of the service] for fast days -- how [is it performed]? They take out the Ark to the open space of the city, and place burnt ashes on it. And they would not take turns (מתחלפין (see Lieberman)); rather, one person would sit and watch over it the whole day. The Elder who is with them says before them words of encouragement: "My sons, a person may be ashamed for his fellow, but a person should not be ashamed for his deeds. It is better that a person be ashamed for his fellow, and let him and his children not persist in hunger, and so it says (Is. 58:3), 'Why did we fast and You did not see? We afflicted our souls, and You did not know?' What can be inferred from this? 'Because on your fast day, [you pursue your business and exact all your payments]. Because you fast for strife and contentiousness, etc. Is such the fast that I desire, a day that a person afflicts his soul, etc.? Rather, this is the fast that I choose: To unfasten the bonds of wickedness, etc.' (Is. 58:3-6.) If there is a sheretz in a person's hand, even if he were to immerse it in the Shiloah, and in all the waters of Creation, he would not be purified. [But] if he casts a sheretz from his hand, he may immerse himself in [a mikveh of] forty seah of water, [and his immersion] is effective. And thus it says (Prov. 28:13), 'He who confesses and forsakes [his transgressions] will be granted mercy.' And it says (Lam. 3:41), 'Let us lift up our hearts with our palms, etc.'"
text.0_Chapter, 8_Tosefta: He recites before them twenty-four [blessings], eighteen that are [recited] every day, [and] he would add six. The seventh: In the name of Summachos they said, "Who humbles the haughty," where is it [placed]? Between "Who redeems Israel" and "Who heals the sick." They answer "amen" for each and every blessing. They [sound the shofar with] tekiah, teruah, and tekiah. So were they accustomed in the outlying areas, [but] in the Temple, what did they recite? "Blessed art Thou, Hashem, God of Israel, from Eternity until Eternity," and they do not answer "amen" in the Temple. From where is it derived that they do not answer "amen' in the Temple? As it is said (Neh. 9:5), "Arise and bless Hashem your God, etc." From where is it derived, for each and every blessing and each and every prayer? A it is said (ibid.), "Exalted over every blessing and prayer." [Meaning] over each and every blessing, and over each and every prayer.
text.0_Chapter, 9_Tosefta: For [the conclusion of] the first [of the six blessings], he recites, "Blessed be Hashem, God of Israel, from Eternity until Eternity. Blessed be the Redeemer of Israel." And they answer after him, "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom, etc." And the sexton of the congregation says to them, "Sound tekiah!" The Priests sounded the tekiah, and he returns and says to them, "He Who answered Abraham on Mount Moriah, He will answer you and He will listen to the sound of your wails on this day." They [then] sound tekiah and teruah. For the second [blessing], he recites, "Blessed be Hashem, God of Israel, from Eternity until Eternity. Blessed be He Who remembers the forgotten." And they answer after him, "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom, [etc.]." The sexton of the congregation says to them, "Sound teruah, sons of Aaron!" They sounded teruah, and he returns and says to them, "He Who answered Moses and our forefathers at the Sea of Reeds, He will answer you and He will listen to the sound of your wails on this day." They [then] sound tekiah and teruah and tekiah. One tekiah and one teruah until everyone finishes. Thus did Rabbi Chalafta conduct [the service] in Tzippori, and Rabbi Chanina ben Teradion in Sachni, but when the matter came before the Sages, they said, "They only conducted [the service] in this manner in the eastern gates [of the Temple]."
text.1_Chapter, 0_Tosefta: Four [Priestly] watches ascended from the exile: Yod'ayah, Charum, Pashchor, and Eimar. The prophets who were in Jerusalem divided them and installed them*וחלקום והעמידום (GR"A), and made them into twenty-four watches, and they [inscribed their names on lots and] mixed them up and tossed them inside the ballot box. And Yod'ayah came and took out five, and with his own, behold, he had six. Charum came and took five, and with his own, behold, he had six. Pashchor came and took five, and with his own, behold, he had six. Eimar came and took five, and with his own, behold, he had six. And thus the prophets distributed [the watches] among them, for even should Yehoyariv (the head of the watches (see 1 Chron. 24:7) come up from the exile, Yod'ayah will not be displaced from its position; rather Yod'ayah will be the main [watch] and Yehoyariv will be secondary. The heads of the watches stood up and they affixed themselves to ancestral houses (see Taan. 2:6).
text.1_Chapter, 1_Tosefta: Every [Priestly] watch has*יש בו, not שיש בו ("that has") (Kometz Minchah) four, five, six, seven, eight, [or] nine [members]. A watch that has four: Three sacrifice for two days [each], and one sacrifices on one day*i.e., for a total of seven days for that watch; and so too for each of the subsequent calculations. A watch that has five: Three sacrifice for two days [each], and two sacrifice on one day. A watch that has six: Five sacrifice on five days, and one sacrifices for two days. A watch that has seven: Each and every one sacrifices on his [particular] day. A watch that has eight: Six sacrifice on six days and two sacrifice on one day. A watch that has nine: Five sacrifice on five days, and four sacrifice on two days. And there are those among them who affixed themselves permanently. One who comes [to serve] on Shabbat comes on Shabbat permanently. [One who comes] after Shabbat, [comes] after Shabbat permanently. And there are those among them who draw lots*שמגרילין not שמגדילין (GR"A) once a month; there are those among them who draw lots once a week; and there are those among them who draw lots on each and every watch.
text.1_Chapter, 2_Tosefta: Whoever knows his watch and his ancestral house*in other words, he knows which week his ancestral house is scheduled to perform the Temple service, and which day of the week his watch is scheduled (Minchat Yitzchak), and he is from one of the permanent ancestral houses, he is only forbidden [from drinking wine] on that same day (i.e., since there is no doubt when he will be called into service (see Taan. 2:7)). Whoever knows his watch but does not know his ancestral house, and he is from one of the permanent ancestral houses, he is forbidden for the whole week. Anyone who does not know either his watch or his ancestral house, and he is from one of the permanent ancestral houses, he is forbidden for the whole month. Rebbi says, I say that this one should be forbidden forever, for his repair is his ruin (see San. 22b:11).
text.1_Chapter, 3_Tosefta: For what reason are the men of the watch permitted to drink wine by night but not by day? For if the service weighs heavily*תכבד העבודה (see Ex.5:9) on the men of the ancestral house, they will rely upon them. The men of the ancestral house [drink wine] neither by day nor by night because they are permanently in service.
text.1_Chapter, 4_Tosefta: The men of the watch and the men of the "post"*אנשי מעמד (" a division of popular representatives deputed to accompany the daily services in the Temple with prayers, and also a corresponding division in the country towns, answering to the divisions (guards, v. מִשְׁמָר) of priests and Levites") (Jastrow) are forbidden to cut their hair or to launder their clothes [during their week of service (Taan. 2:7)], both from the time that the Temple was destroyed and before the Temple was destroyed. Rabbi Yosei says, from the time that the Temple was destroyed, they are permitted because [the destruction] is [itself a source of] mourning for them. § On Monday and Thursday, an individual [who takes upon himself to fast on behalf of the public] may sit*יחיד יושב (see Lieberman) for a public fast, and on those days the Batei Dinim (courts) sit in the towns, and on those days they enter the synagogues and read [from the Torah], and on those days they interrupt the [regular] reading of the Megillah (see Meg. 3:4).
text.1_Chapter, 5_Tosefta:
What is the difference between a communal fast and an individual fast? On a communal fast, they may eat and drink while it is still daytime, which is not the case with an individual fast. On a communal fast, they are forbidden from working, bathing, and anointing, and wearing shoes, and marital relations, which is not the case with an individual fast. On a communal fast, they enter the synagogues, which is not the case with an individual fast. On a communal fast, they take out the Ark to the open space of the city, which is not the case with an individual fast. On a communal fast, they pray with twenty-four blessings [during the Amidah], which is not the case with an individual fast. On a communal fast, the Priests raise their hands four times in a day, which is not the case with an individual fast. On a communal fast, they do not interrupt [the regular service of] the Festivals written in Megillat [Ta'anit] (Taan. 12a:9), which is not the case with an individual fast.
It so happened that they decreed that there be a fast on Chanukah in Lod. They informed Rabbi Eliezer, and he cut his hair; Rabbi Yehoshua, and he bathed (i.e., to show that they did not accept the fast). Rabbi Yehoshua said to them, go out and fast [in penitence] for that which you have [already] fasted (i.e., for having fasted on Chanukah, which is prohibited).
As long as Rabban Gamaliel was alive, the halacha followed according to his words. After the death of Rabban Gamaliel, Rabbi Yehoshua sought to abolish his words. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri stood up on his legs and said, "I see that the body must follow the head*i.e., the subsequent generations must follow the rulings of the earlier generations (see Eruvin 41a:6); note that the preceding portion of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's oration is in Aramaic; the remainder is in Mishnaic Hebrew. As long as Rabban Gamaliel was alive, the halacha followed according to his words. Now that he is dead, you (pl.) are seeking to abolish his words?" Said Rabbi Yehoshua, "We hear you. The halacha will be established according to the words of Rabban Gamaliel." And there was no one who contested his words.
text.1_Chapter, 6_Tosefta: As to Shabbats and Festivals, it is permitted to fast before them and after them. Why are these ones (i.e., the days written in Megillat Ta'anit) forbidden while those ones (Shabbats and Festivals) are permitted? Those ones are the words of the Torah, and the words of the Torah do not require [additional] stringency, [while] these ones are the words of the scribes, and the words of the scribes do require [additional] stringency. Abba Yosei ben Dosai said in the name of Rabbi Yosei HaGalili, one who takes an oath to fast on Erev Shabbat, behold, that is a false oath.
text.1_Chapter, 7_Tosefta: And [when] the Ninth of Av falls out on Erev Shabbat (Friday), a person eats the equivalent of an egg's bulk and drinks the equivalent of an egg's bulk*alt., "eats even the equivalent of an egg's bulk and drinks the equivalent of an egg's bulk" (MS Erfurt); alt., "eats the equivalent of an egg's bulk and even drinks the equivalent of an egg's bulk" (MS Vienna; GR"A), so that [Shabbat] does not come in while he is in a state of affliction, the words of Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Yosei says, behold, he must fast and complete [his fast]. Rabbi Yosei said to him, "Do you not agree that when the Ninth of Av falls out after Shabbat, that they [only] eat and drink while it is still day? What is the difference between entering into Shabbat in a state of affliction, and leaving Shabbat in a state of affliction?" He said to him, "No. If you are saying so in regards to [the fast commencing after Shabbat], when they can eat and drink the whole day, can you say the same in regards to [the fast commencing the day before Shabbat], when they can only eat and drink with the coming of nightfall?"
text.1_Chapter, 8_Tosefta: Just as they blow the shofar for the rains during the other years of the agricultural cycle (lit., "the week"), so too they blow the shofar for them on the Sabbatical Year for the sake of sustaining others*e.g., the poor, who are permitted to take produce from the fields during the Sabbatical Year (Minchat Yitzchak). And they blow the shofar for the trees during the Passover season, and for the cisterns and for the ditches and for the caves [that have not been filled with water] during the Sukkot season. If they do not have water to drink, they blow the shofar for them (i.e., the rains) immediately. And what do they mean by "immediately"? Monday and Thursday. And in all of these cases, they only blow the shofar on their account in the same province.
text.1_Chapter, 9_Tosefta: A pestilence where there is an interruption (i.e., a full day passes without fatalities): Even if there are three deaths in one day [after the interruption], one after another, this is not considered a pestilence [for purposes of fasting (see Taan. 3:4)]. A pestilence where there is no interruption: Even if there are three deaths over three days, one after another, behold, this is a considered a pestilence. Diphtheria: If there are any deaths from it, they blow the shofar on its account; if not, they do not blow the shofar on its account. They blow the shofar on account of the govay (a species of locust) in any amount, because this is a plague that is likely to spread (Taan. 3:5). Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says, even on account of the chagav (edible locusts). Armies passing from place to place: Even [if it is] an "army of peace," they blow the shofar on its account, and needless to say, if it is an "army of retribution." And there is no greater example than an "army of peace" than Pharoah Neco, and it swept away that righteous man, he being [King] Josiah (2 Chr. 35:20-25): "[Neco] sent messengers to him, saying, 'What have I to do with you, etc.'" "It is God’s will that I hurry" -- [meaning,] from the mouth of the Holy I am ascending [to battle]. "Restrain yourself [from interfering, for elohim is with me]" -- that is the language of idolatry (see Taan. 22b:2). "But Josiah would not turn his face from him, but he costumed himself [in armor], etc.," "And archers shot King Josiah, etc.," "[And Jerusalem] went into mourning over Josiah, etc.," "And Jeremiah composed laments for Josiah, etc." Here is the exposition of the matter (Lam. 4:20): "The breath of our life, God's anointed one, [was captured in their traps]." And for all of these, they only blow the shofar on their account in the same province. If [a plague] happened in Syria, they do not blow the shofar on its account [in Judea].
text.1_Chapter, 10_Tosefta:
A city that is surrounded by Gentile [troops], or by a river, and so too a ship foundering on the sea (Taan. 3:7), and so too an individual who is being pursued by Gentiles, or by bandits, or by an evil spirit -- they do not have the right to afflict themselves by fasting, so as not to break their strength. And so too would Rabbi Yosei say, an individual does not have the right to afflict himself with fasting lest [this cause] the community to fall, as they may need to sustain him [as a result of his fasting].
*According to MS Erfurt, the third chapter of Taanit starts here, and the fourth chapter starts where the third chapter of the printed version commences.It so happened that they told a certain pious man to pray for the rains to fall, and the rains fell. They said to him, "Just as you prayed for the rains to fall, so too you should now pray for them to cease." He said to them, "Go out and take a look. If a man can stand at Keren Ophil and dangle*ומקשקש; alt., וישכשך ("dip") (GR"A; see Taan. 22b:17); alt., משקשק ("make noise with") (MS Erfurt; Y. Taan. III.9.9 ) his leg in the Kidron Brook, we will pray that the rains not fall, but we are certain that the Place will never bring [another] flood, as it is said (Gen. 9:15), 'And never again shall the waters become a flood, [to bring all flesh to ruin]'; [and it says] (Is. 54:9), 'For to me this [eternal kindness] is like the waters of Noah, which I swore [would never again pass over the earth].'" Rabbi Meir says, a flood of water there will not be, but a flood of fire and of brimstone there will be, in the same way that it was brought upon the Sodomites, as it is said (Gen. 19:24), "And God rained upon Sodom [and Gomorrah fire and brimstone]." Rabbi Yehuda says, a flood for "all flesh" there will not be, but an "individual" flood there will be. How so? One who fell into the sea, [or] his ship sank in the sea, and he died, behold, that is his [individual] flood. Rabbi Yosei says, a flood of water there will not be, but a flood of pestilence to the Gentiles (alt., "to the nations of the world" (MS Vienna")) in the days of the Messiah there will be, as it is said (Zech. 11:10-11), "And I took (or 'will take') My staff of Grace [and cleft it asunder, to annual the covenant that I entered into with the nations]." What does it [then] say, "And it was (or 'will be') annulled on that day."
text.1_Chapter, 11_Tosefta:
Pregnant and nursing women fast on the Ninth of Av, and Yom Kippur, and on the three public fast days, but they would not fast on the remainder of the fast days. Not that they were allowed to indulge in delicacies*ולא שיענגו את עצמן בתפנוקין (Jastrow); rather, they eat and drink as much as is required to sustain the newborn. One who was fasting for a sick person, and he recovered, [or] due to a matter of distress, and it passed -- behold, he should [nonetheless] complete his fast. Behold, one who was fasting and forgot, and ate and drank, [nonetheless] completes his fast. One who goes from a place where they are fasting to a place where they are not fasting -- behold, this one completes his fast. One who entered a city and found that they are fasting -- behold, this one fasts along with them.
What is the "Great Hallel" (see Taan. 3:9)? (Ps. 136:2-3), "Give thanks to the God of gods, [for His mercy endures forever]; Give thanks to the Lord of lords, [for His mercy endures forever]."
text.2_Chapter, 0_Tosefta: On three occasions, [the Priests] lift up their hands four times in a day -- at dawn, at noon*presumably referring to the mussaf prayer, as per Taan. 4:1 (see Minchat Yitzchak), at minchah, and at neilah, the words of Rabbi Meir. And the Sages say, at minchah and neilah there was not the lifting of the hands, as it is said (Deut. 18:5), "[For God chose him (i.e., the Priest) from all your tribes] for standing and administering in the name of God, him and his sons, all the days." "His sons" are juxtaposed with "him": Just as he stands and lifts up his hands in the morning, his sons also stand and lift up their hands in the morning.
text.2_Chapter, 1_Tosefta: Moses instituted eight watches for the Priesthood, and eight watches for the Levites. Once David and Samuel the Seer rose up, they made them into twenty-four Priestly watches and twenty-four Levitical watches, as it is said (1 Chr. 9:22), "[David and Samuel the Seer] established them in their office of trust" -- these are the Priestly and Levitical watches. The prophets that were in Jerusalem rose up and affixed there twenty-four posts [of Israelites] corresponding to the twenty-four Priestly and Levitical watches, as it is said (Num. 28:2), "Command the Children of Israel and say to them, My sacrifices, My food ... [you are to be vigilant in offering Me at their appointed time]." It is impossible to say that all of Israel [was tasked with this duty]; rather, it teaches that the agent of a person is like himself.
text.2_Chapter, 2_Tosefta: [When] the time arrived for the Priestly and Levitical watch, they would ascend to Jerusalem. And the Israelites who were in the same watch, [but] who were unable to ascend to Jerusalem, would assemble in their cities and read the Act of Creation (i.e., the beginning of Genesis), and they would desist from working that entire week. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says, [the absence of] Priests and Levites and musical instruments prevents the [Temple] service [from being performed]. On the first of Nissan, there is no minchah and no neila, on account of there being a mussaf offering and a wood offering on that [day].
text.2_Chapter, 3_Tosefta: A large portion (i.e., more than three verses of the Act of Creation) is read by two [men of the post], and a small one by an individual, during the morning service and during mussaf, the words of Rabbi Meir.*In Taan. 4:3, Rabbi Meir's opinion is presented anonymously, and the opinion of the Sages (which follows) is not mentioned. And the Sages say, any [day] in which there is a mussaf [offering], they they read [the Act of Creation] during mussaf; and any [day] in which there is no mussaf [offering], they do not read it during mussaf. For the morning service and for mussaf, they enter the synagogues and read, and for minchah they read (i.e., recite) by heart. Rabbi Yehuda says, an individual does not read by heart; rather, they enter the synagogues and read by heart in the same way that they read the Shema (see Tos. Sotah 6:2).
text.2_Chapter, 4_Tosefta: Why did they see fit to specify the times for the wood offering of the Priests and the people (Taan. 4:5)? [They said,] when the returning exiles did not find wood in the [Temple] chamber, those [families] stood up and were generous with their own wood, and handed it over to the public, and thus the prophets were generous with them, such that even if the [Temple] chamber is filled with wood, and even if [there is sufficient] wood from the public, that those [families may continue to] stand up and be generous with their own wood. There should not be a sacrifice that is offered up, except if [the wood pile] started with their wood, as it is said (Neh. 10:35), "We have cast lots to bring the wood offering, etc.," and it says (Ezra 7:10), "For Ezra had prepared his heart [to expound upon the Torah of God, etc.]."
text.2_Chapter, 5_Tosefta: [On] those days (of the wood offerings) it is forbidden regarding eulogizing [and fasting, (both) whether when the Temple was destroyed or when the Temple was not destroyed]. Rabbi Yosi says: when the Temple was destroyed we permit it because one is mourning for them. Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok said: I was among the descendants of S'nav, the son of Benjamin, and when Tisha B'Av fell on Shabbat and we delayed it until after Shabbat we would fast, but not complete [it].
text.2_Chapter, 6_Tosefta: What are the "children of the pestle-stealers" (b'nei gonvei eli) and the "children of the fig-cutters" (b'nei kotzei k'tziyot) (Taan. 4:5)? It was that at the time that the kings of Greece stationed border guards on the roads so that [the pilgrims] would not ascend to Jerusalem, in the same way that Jeroboam had stationed them. Whoever was fit [to enter the Temple] and sin-fearing in that generation would take his first fruits, cover them up with packing-figs, and place them in vessels, and take a basket and a pestle on his shoulder, and ascend. When he arrived to that same guard-post, they said to him, "Where are you going?" He said, "To make these two [clumps of] packing-figs into two rounds of fig-cake with that mortar over there that is before me, [and] with this pestle that is on my shoulder." As soon as he passed that same guard-post, he adorned [the first-fruits] and brought them up to Jerusalem.
text.2_Chapter, 7_Tosefta: What is the meaning of the "children of Salmai, the Netophatite"?*בני סלמאי הנטופתי. Per Lieberman, this refers to the genealogical list at I Chron. 2:54, "The children of Salma: Bethlehem, the Netophatites, etc." (בני שלמא בית לחם ונטופתי). But note the different orthography (סלמאי vs. שלמא). Also notably, while the previous Tosefta (expounding on the "children of the pestle-stealers" and "children of the fig-cutters") relates directly to families who are identified in the Mishnah as being designated to bring the wood offering, the "children of Salmai" are not referenced. It was at the time that the kings of Greece stationed border guards on the roads so that [the pilgrims] would not ascend to Jerusalem, in the same way that Jeroboam ben Nebat had stationed them. Whoever was sin-fearing and fit [to enter the Temple] in that generation would bring two logs of wood and fashion them into a type of ladder (sulam), and place them on his shoulder, and ascend. When he arrived to that same guard-post, he said to him, "Where are you going?" He said, "To take two doves from that dovecote over there that is before me, with this ladder that is on my shoulder." As soon as he passed that same guard-post, he broke up [the logs of wood] and brought them up to Jerusalem, and according to how they delivered themselves on account of the Torah and on account of the commandments, therefore it turned out that they had a good name and a good remembrance for all time. And about them it says (Prov. 10:7), "The memory of the righteous shall be for a blessing," and about Jeroboam ben Nebat and his colleagues it says (ibid.), "And the name of the wicked shall rot."
text.2_Chapter, 8_Tosefta: [From where do we derive that the Second Temple was also destroyed on the Ninth of Av (Taan. 4:6)?] Rabbi Yosei says, a meritorious matter is brought about on an auspicious day, and a deleterious matter on an inauspicious day (Taan. 29a:11 (Steinsaltz tr.)). When they destroyed the First Temple, it was at the conclusion of Shabbat, and the conclusion of the Sabbatical year, and it was the watch of Yehoyariv, and the Ninth of Av. And so too with the Second [Temple]. And [at the time of both destructions] the Levites were standing on their platform and saying (Ps. 94:23), "And He will turn their iniquity [and their evil] upon them, etc." In the future, when the Temple will be rebuilt, what does it say (1 Chr. 16:36), "Blessed be Hashem, God of Israel, from Eternity until Eternity," [and] (Ps. 72:18-19), "He performs wonders alone, and blessed is His glorious name [forever], etc."
text.2_Chapter, 9_Tosefta: "On the ninth of the [fourth] month the [walls of the] city were breached" (Jer. 39:2) -- regarding the Second [Temple] and regarding the First [Temple]. And [it says] (2 Kings 25:9), "[In the fifth month,] on the seventh [of the month ... Nabuzaradan ... came to Jerusalem and he burnt the House of the Lord"]" (see Taan. 29a:8). If it is said*The reference here to Jer. 52:6 must be erroneous, for that verse states, "On the ninth day of the fourth month, the famine was severe in the city.", "on the seventh of the month," why is it [also] said, "on the ninth of the month"? [And] if it is said, "on the ninth of the month," why is it [also] said, "on the seventh of the month"? Rather, on the seventh of the month, the nations conquered the Heichal, and they carried away the pillars, and the Sea [of Solomon (1 Kings 7:23-26)], and the slaughtering-stalls. And they were working on its demolition on the seventh, eighth, and ninth, until the turning of the day (i.e., twilight). And thus it says (Jer. 6:4), "Alas for us, for the day is turning, for the shadows of the evening are stretching out." At evening time, they set fire to it, and it was burned with the setting of the sun, on the tenth of the month.
text.2_Chapter, 10_Tosefta: Whenever it is the meal [before] the Ninth of Av, it is prohibited to eat meat or to drink wine, and it is forbidden to eat two cooked dishes, and it is forbidden to wash and to anoint, and any meal that is not [the meal before] the Ninth of Av, it is permitted to eat meat, and to drink wine, and it is permitted to eat two cooked dishes, and it is permitted to wash and to anoint. Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yosei in the name of his father [says], any time that it is permitted to eat, it is permitted to wash one's face, hands, and feet. And one may not greet chaverim (i.e., those punctilious in observance) on the Ninth of Av. But to a common person, [one may return a greeting] in an undertone. They decreed this from the Ninth of Av until the conclusion of the Ninth of Av. Once the Ninth of Av has passed, they are permitted [to greet] everyone.
text.2_Chapter, 11_Tosefta: [If] the Ninth of Av falls on Shabbat, a person may eat all he requires, and drink all he requires, and place upon table even such a feast as that of Solomon in his time, and he may not withhold anything from himself.
text.2_Chapter, 12_Tosefta: The same days [that now are fast days] will in the future be festive days for Israel, as it is said (Zech. 8:19), "Thus said God, the fast of the fourth month, etc., [will be for joy and happiness and cheerful festivals for the House of Judah]," and all who mourn for her (i.e., Jerusalem) in this world will be joyful in the world to come, as it is said (Is. 66:10), "Rejoice with Jerusalem and be gladdened with her, all those who love her, etc."
